title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity: Sparsity: and At

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ("40 variants of 30B MoE models and 3.4B dense models trained on a 1 trillion token dataset")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The experimental sections describe MoE models with 15B total / 2.54B activated parameters ("15A2B", Table 1, Table 7) and 1.7B dense models (Table 2, Table 7), trained on 400B tokens (MoE), 400B/1T/3.5T tokens (dense), drawn from a 4T-token corpus. The abstract's '30B MoE', '3.4B dense' and '1 trillion token dataset' contradict every other statement of model size and data budget in the paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph beginning "In this work, we investigate gating mechanisms..." items (i) and (ii)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The intro claims "applying key layer gating (G3) yields superior performance improvements compared to SDPA or value gating, reducing PPL by up to 0.3 and improving MMLU significantly" and "gating at G3 also leads to better training stability". Table 1 shows key gating (row 7, G3) is essentially at baseline level (PPL 6.016 vs baseline 6.026, HellaSwag 72.88 below baseline), whereas SDPA gating (row 5, G1) is best (PPL 5.761). All stability/scaling experiments (Table 2) use SDPA gating, not G3. The paper's own 'Practical Recommendation' also says to use G1.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 1 (middle) tables of PPL and % PPL ∆
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The middle table lists key gating as the lowest PPL (5.75) and SDPA gating as 5.95, contradicting Table 1 (SDPA 5.761 best, key 6.016 essentially baseline) and contradicting the figure's own caption ("Gating after SDPA (G1) yields the best overall results"). The accompanying '% PPL ∆' table is also incoherent: SDPA and value are given identical -0.26% despite different PPLs, and key/query/dense are shown as positive (worse) which does not match the listed PPL values.

In the diagram G1 is attached to W_v (the value projection) and G2 is absent, while the text defines G1 as the gate on the SDPA output and G2 as the gate after the value projection. The diagram therefore contradicts the position definitions used throughout the paper.

The text states "both baselines and gating variants frequently encounter convergence issues (row 6, 12), with some gating models diverging silently" and "gating alone does not consistently improve stability at extreme hyperparameters" / "training instabilities still occur under substantially increased learning rates". Table 2 shows no diverging gated run: rows 6 and 12 are both baselines, while gated runs at LR 8e-3 (rows 10 and 14) converge and give the best results (7.325 and 7.078). The claim contradicts the reported evidence.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ("gating alone does not fully resolve training instabilities at larger learning rates, requiring additional normalization strategies")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: No experiment in the paper shows a gated model failing at higher learning rate; Table 2 rows 10 and 14 show gated models training successfully at 8e-3 where the baseline degrades (row 6) or diverges (row 12). Sandwich norm is only tested on baselines, so the claim that gating 'requires additional normalization strategies' is unsupported.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.3 opening vs. Introduction / Section 5.2 / Appendix A.4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 4.3 says "these phenomena persist to a non-trivial degree in some layers and models. This suggests gating partially alleviates but does not entirely resolve attention sink issues", while the Introduction states the models "exhibit no attention sink", Section 5.2 says "sparse gating after SDPA eliminates attention sinks", and Appendix A.4 reports "no significant attention sink phenomenon is observed in any layer". These statements are mutually contradictory.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 4 row (5) 'Value Elementwise Gate' GSM8k vs Table 1 row (6) and Table 3 row (3)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 4 reports GSM8k = 51.33 for value elementwise gating, while Table 1 (row 6, 'v Elementwise G_2') and Table 3 (row 3, 'V Elementwise Gate') both report 53.97 for the same model (all other numbers — PPL 5.820, HellaSwag 74.38, MMLU 59.17 — match).

The caption states "The majority of gating scores fall mostly between 0.4 and 0.7, indicating less sparsity. Differences in sparsity across gating positions are diminished." This contradicts Section 4.2 and Table 4, which report mean gating scores of 0.116 (SDPA elementwise), 0.172 (headwise), 0.221 (value), 0.271 (head-shared) and claim "a high concentration near 0, indicating substantial sparsity" and that sparsity differs markedly across positions.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 4 row (7) 'F-Attn' (0.451) vs Appendix Figure 6 ('attn_output_gate_wo_sparsity ... mean: 0.481')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The same quantity (mean first-token attention score of the NS-sigmoid / no-sparsity gating model) is reported as 0.451 in Table 4 and 0.481 in Figure 6; all other configurations match exactly (0.467, 0.048, 0.297, 0.301), so one of the two values is wrong. Furthermore, Section 4.3 (iii) claims NS-sigmoid "intensifies both massive activations and attention sink", yet Table 4's numbers (M-Act 892, F-Attn 0.451) are both lower than the baseline (1053, 0.467).

predicted_errors.error_location: Eq. (9) NS-sigmoid vs Appendix A.5 / Figure 7 gate-value table
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Eq. (9), NS-sigmoid(x) = 0.5 + 0.5·sigmoid(x), "constrains the gating scores between [0.5, 1.0]". The reported per-layer statistics for 'attn_output_gate_wo_sparsity' in Figure 7 list minimum gate values of ~0.0–0.15, which is impossible under the stated formula.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 1, 'Added Param' column for rows (12) and (13) (head-shared gating)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Both head-shared variants have the same gating score shape (n × d_k), so the added gate parameters (d_model × d_k per layer) must be identical, yet row (12) reports 201M and row (13) reports 25M. Moreover, with d_model=2048, d_k=128, 24 layers, head-shared gating adds ≈6.3M parameters, so neither figure is consistent with the stated shapes (the 201M and 25M values correspond to the head-specific q×d_k and k×d_k gates of rows 5 and 6).

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction ("both our dense and MoE models (trained on 3.5T tokens) exhibit no attention sink") and Section 5.2 ("dense (1B-parameter) and MoE (15B-parameter) models ... trained on 3.5T tokens")
